title: Nasopharyngeal carriage and antibiotic susceptibility patterns of streptococcus pneumoniae, haemophilus influenzae, moraxella catarrhalis and staphylococcus aureus among urban Ugandan children post-PCV10 introduction: a cross-sectional study.
ehr_evidence: Nasopharyngeal samples were collected from the children by using single sterile swabs... sent to the Clinical Microbiology Laboratory... an interviewer-administered questionnaire was used to collect clinical and demographic data.
summary: Cross-sectional study assessing nasopharyngeal carriage and antibiotic susceptibility patterns of four respiratory bacterial pathogens among urban Ugandan children 5 years post-PCV10 vaccine introduction.
key_findings: Carriage was significantly associated with a history of antibiotic use (p=0.0159) and respiratory symptoms (p=0.0003).
S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, and S. aureus carriage prevalences were 46% (90/194), 21% (40/194), 7% (14/194), and 6% (12/194), respectively.
Species co-carriage occurred in 17% (32/194) of children, predominantly S. pneumoniae + H. influenzae (23 children).
Pneumococci showed high resistance to cotrimoxazole (100%), erythromycin (76%), and tetracycline (52%), with 42% being multidrug-resistant.
H. influenzae isolates were highly resistant to cotrimoxazole (100%) and tetracycline (75%).
Post-PCV10 introduction was associated with decreased pneumococcal carriage and increased H. influenzae carriage compared to pre-PCV10 data, alongside increased antibiotic resistance.
captured_features: antibiotic susceptibility testing (MIC and disc diffusion)
data_source_type: primary microbiological sampling and laboratory testing with questionnaire survey
population: children 6-60 months of age attending outpatient clinic at Mulago Hospital Assessment Centre, Kampala, Uganda
exposure_domain: PCV10 vaccination status, history of antibiotic use, respiratory symptoms, household crowding
limitations: 52 isolates not recovered due to freeze-thaw episodes and fastidious nature of bacteria, reducing sample size
isolates collected from sick children without clinical evaluation to determine pathogenic relevance
